clue.text: Oil production in South American country's risky

indicators.note: a production is something made or worked up, so the word before it is reworked into a new order
one piece is placed inside another, the country's name wrapping round the reworked letters

blocks.note: Peru plus the possessive S
the word oil rearranged

explanation.surface: A news line about oil extraction in Peru or Venezuela being a hazardous business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Production' looks like oil output, but it is the signal to rearrange the word oil.
explanation.definitionFit: Perilous means full of danger, a close synonym of risky as an adjective.

clue.text: Terrible being caught out of control

indicators.note: taking something out of a word removes those letters from it

blocks.note: to direct is to control
CT is a cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught

explanation.surface: Someone describes a dreadful creature that has been captured and is running wild.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove CT from DIRECT to leave DIRE. Cricket scorecards write 'ct' for a batsman caught out.
explanation.definitionFit: Dire is a common adjective for something dreadful or extremely bad, a direct synonym of terrible.

clue.text: Fix grate

blocks.note: first meaning: an awkward predicament, a jam
second meaning: to rub harshly against a surface

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an instruction to repair a fireplace grate; both words are in fact definitions, the first a noun and the second a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrape is a tricky situation, like a fix, and to scrape is to rasp or abrade, like grating.

clue.text: Vicar has free love to go round!

indicators.note: letters set free are released from their order and can be rearranged

blocks.note: REV is short for Reverend, a vicar's title
love rearranged

explanation.surface: A scandalised exclamation about a clergyman embracing free love so that it can spread around.
explanation.definitionFit: To revolve is to turn or circle about an axis, an infinitive matching 'to go round'.

clue.text: Ring nice doctor about catching the odd cold

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the preceding word is altered in order
the odd ones are the first, third and further odd-numbered positions of the next word
something catching another holds it inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: nice rearranged
RE means about or concerning
the first and third letters of cold

explanation.surface: Someone phones a pleasant GP about a sniffle that has been doing the rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: ENCI followed by R(CL)E. 'Doctor' looks like a noun for the GP but is a verb telling you to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To encircle is to surround completely, which is what ring means as a verb.

clue.text: Cancelled new aids to students in arrears

indicators.note: making something new means remaking it, so the following word is rearranged

blocks.note: aids rearranged
L is a learner driver, so two learners are students
money in arrears is owed

explanation.surface: A grant for indebted students has been scrapped.
explanation.walkthrough: L is the learner plate on a British car, so LL is a common way to clue students or learners.
explanation.definitionFit: A goal or claim that is disallowed has been ruled invalid, much like being cancelled.

clue.text: Kingdoms have male order in monarchs

indicators.note: putting letters in order means arranging them afresh, so the preceding word is rearranged
one piece sits inside another, here inside the monarchs

blocks.note: R stands for Rex or Regina, king or queen; two of them are monarchs
male rearranged

explanation.surface: A remark that kingdoms keep a male line of succession among their rulers.
explanation.walkthrough: R(EALM)S. R is the royal cipher letter, as in ER for Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: A realm is a kingdom or the territory ruled by a monarch, so the plural matches kingdoms.

clue.text: Average doctor has nothing to go on about

indicators.note: the doctor has, that is holds within, the next piece

blocks.note: a medic is a doctor
O looks like zero, nothing
RE means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A grumble about a run-of-the-mill GP who has no grounds to keep talking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has' here means holds inside, and 'to go on' means the last piece is placed after the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Mediocre means only ordinary or middling in quality, an adjective like average.

clue.text: Local model's dismissed as unsophisticated

indicators.note: something dismissed is sent away, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: a local is a native of a place
the Model T Ford gives T for model

explanation.surface: A provincial fashion model is written off as too green for the big time.
explanation.walkthrough: NATIVE without the T. The Model T was Henry Ford's famous early car.
explanation.definitionFit: Naive describes someone innocent and lacking worldly experience, which is what unsophisticated means.

clue.text: Leather cover

blocks.note: first meaning: an animal skin used for leather
second meaning: to conceal or screen from view

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a leather cover for a book or seat; the two words are separate meanings, the second a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A hide is the skin of an animal tanned for leather, and to hide something is to conceal it.

clue.text: Very bad for sailor having no time to get fit

blocks.note: AB, able seaman, is a sailor
O for nought, none
a minute is a unit of time
fit and able are synonyms

explanation.surface: It's terrible for a seaman to have no time to keep in shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No time' looks like one idea but splits into O for no and MIN for time.
explanation.definitionFit: Abominable means dreadful or awful, an intensified synonym of very bad.

clue.text: Comfort thus on a shoestring

blocks.note: so and thus both mean in this way
a shoelace is a shoestring

explanation.surface: Finding consolation while living on a tight budget.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On a shoestring' is the idiom for on very little money; here a shoestring is just a lace.
explanation.definitionFit: Solace is consolation in distress, a noun synonym of comfort.

clue.text: Support good point when upheld by federation

indicators.note: held up in a down clue means the letters are read from bottom to top
held by the next word means sitting inside it

blocks.note: G is short for good
E is a compass point, east
an alliance is a federation

explanation.surface: A union pledges backing on a good point once the federation upholds it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upheld' does double duty: 'up' turns the letters upward in this down clue and 'held by' puts them inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Allegiance is loyal backing for a cause or ruler, a noun sense of support.

clue.text: Singer's against having a company's back catalogue

indicators.note: going back means the preceding words are read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: V for versus, against
A plus CO, the abbreviation for company
a catalogue is a list

explanation.surface: A singer opposes a record label's reissue of their old recordings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back catalogue' is a music-industry phrase, but here 'back' turns 'a company' around and the catalogue is just a list.
explanation.definitionFit: A vocalist is a performer who sings, typically with a band, a direct synonym for singer.

clue.text: Don't consume so much — it serves no purpose

definitions.note: a phrase, read as the two words use less
a clause; the answer is the adjective for such a thing

blocks.note: first reading: an instruction to cut back, split as two words
second reading: describing something with no function

explanation.surface: An environmental plea to cut back consumption because it achieves nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer read as two words, USE LESS, is an instruction; read as one, it is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Something useless has no practical value, which is what serving no purpose means.

clue.text: Poor nag's in condition to do nothing

indicators.note: something in poor shape is out of order, so the next word is rearranged
is in places one piece inside the other

blocks.note: a state is a condition
nag rearranged

explanation.surface: A sorry old horse is in no shape to do anything.
explanation.walkthrough: STA(GNA)TE. 'Nag's' is nag is, not a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: To stagnate is to stay inactive and stop developing, matching the infinitive 'to do nothing'.

clue.text: New Labour's following economic trends initially on web

indicators.note: initially points to the starting letters of the words before it
following tells you that piece comes after the ones before it

blocks.note: N is short for new
first letters of economic and trends
labour is work; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A political story about New Labour reacting to economic data, with an online angle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New Labour' looks like the party but splits: N for new and WORK for labour.
explanation.definitionFit: A network is an interconnected mesh of lines or links, which a web is.

clue.text: Check for injury after endless trek

indicators.note: without ends means both the first and last letters are dropped, keeping the middle

blocks.note: trek without its first and last letters
a strain is a muscle injury

explanation.surface: Hikers go to be examined for a pulled muscle after an interminable walk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Check' looks like a medical examination, but it is the definition in its sense of holding back.
explanation.definitionFit: To restrain is to hold back or curb, which is a verb sense of check.

clue.text: Snobbish when having drink without snacks

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the drink wraps round the snacks

blocks.note: to sup is to drink
tuck is British schoolchildren's slang for snacks and sweets

explanation.surface: Someone is sniffy about having a drink with nothing to nibble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' looks like 'lacking', but here it means outside. Tuck is the sweets and snacks of a British school tuck shop.
explanation.definitionFit: Stuck-up is an informal adjective for someone haughty and conceited, which is snobbish.

clue.text: Loud shouting about delay is outrageous

blocks.note: F is forte, loud in music
a lag is a delay
a rant is angry shouting

explanation.surface: Noisy complaining about a hold-up is out of order.
explanation.walkthrough: F is the musical mark for forte. The delay sits between the loud and the shouting in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A flagrant offence is glaringly obvious and shocking, close to outrageous.

clue.text: An amateur Lothario?

blocks.note: first meaning: a non-professional, an outsider to a field
second meaning, playful: a seducer, split as two words

explanation.walkthrough: Lothario is a stock name for a womaniser; the question mark flags reading the answer jokily as two words, a man who lays.
explanation.definitionFit: A layman is someone without professional training, so an amateur in a field.

clue.text: Fashion on street is unexceptional

blocks.note: a mode is a fashion
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: Street fashion is nothing special.
explanation.definitionFit: Modest can mean unremarkable or moderate in size or quality, a sense of unexceptional.

clue.text: Disease might consume boy

indicators.note: to consume is to take in, so one word swallows the other

blocks.note: may and might both express possibility
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A warning that an illness could waste a child away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might' looks like a verb on the surface but is the word MAY.
explanation.definitionFit: A malady is an illness or ailment, a somewhat literary synonym of disease.

clue.text: Domineering girl, after try-out in charge, hacked off everybody

indicators.note: out suggests the word is put out of shape, its letters rearranged
something hacked off has had a piece chopped away, here the final letter
after says that the girl's name follows the preceding piece

blocks.note: try rearranged
a girl's name
IC is short for in charge
all is everybody

explanation.surface: A bossy girl who took charge after an audition annoyed everyone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try-out' and 'hacked off' both read as everyday phrases, but each splits into a word plus its instruction. ALL loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Tyrannical describes ruling oppressively like a tyrant, an intensified form of domineering.

clue.text: Heard German boy being rude

indicators.note: what is heard is spoken, so the answer matches a word's sound rather than its spelling

blocks.note: Kurt is a German boy's name

explanation.surface: Someone overheard a German lad being impolite.
explanation.definitionFit: Curt means abrupt or brusque in speech, a form of rudeness.

clue.text: Complain about second-hand price rise

indicators.note: second points to the letter in position two of the word it is attached to
rising in a down clue means reading letters from the bottom up

blocks.note: C for circa, about
the second letter of hand
PR is a dictionary abbreviation for price

explanation.surface: Grumbling about how much used goods have gone up in price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second-hand' looks like used goods but splits into the second letter of hand.
explanation.definitionFit: To carp is to find fault and grumble persistently, a verb synonym of complain.

clue.text: Racecourse on rocky coast

indicators.note: rocky means unstable, so the letters of the next word are shaken into a new order

blocks.note: the word coast, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A racetrack sited on a craggy shoreline.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is a famous English racecourse in Berkshire, home of Royal Ascot.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a specific racecourse, so the answer is an example of the definition.

clue.text: Lower leg support?

definitions.note: a jokey phrase read as two words, under pin
the verb sense; the clue's question mark covers the whole

blocks.note: first reading: pin is slang for a leg, and under means lower
second meaning: to give a foundation or backing to

explanation.walkthrough: Pins is informal British slang for legs, so 'lower leg' can be an under pin; the question mark flags the jokey reading.
explanation.definitionFit: To underpin is to support from beneath, as with a foundation, and figuratively to back up.
